problem: "The dose is set by output power in watts and time in minutes" is fine for short-wave and microwave, but for ultrasound the dose depends on intensity in W/cm² and the size of the treatment head, not total watts, and also on continuous versus pulsed mode. A student could carry the wrong dose model into an ultrasound question.
fix: Keep power and time for short-wave and microwave. Add: for ultrasound, the dose is given as intensity in W/cm² applied for a time in minutes, and the mode (continuous or pulsed) must be stated.

problem: "Commonly up to about 200 W" understates many short-wave physiotherapy units, which are rated at several hundred watts. The fixed number may be marked wrong if a student quotes 200 W as the machine maximum.
fix: Say "typically a few hundred watts (often 250–400 W, depending on the unit)" instead of a single 200 W figure.

problem: The long wavelength (11 m against a body of about 1.7 m) explains why the body does not block the field, but it is not the whole reason for deep heating. Deep heating also needs low absorption per centimetre, which is true at 27.12 MHz and false at 2450 MHz. As written, a student may think wavelength alone decides penetration depth.
fix: Add one sentence: absorption per centimetre also falls as frequency falls, so at 27.12 MHz little energy is lost in the skin and the rest reaches deep tissue.

problem: "The implant may also be near the return path" is loose wording. A return plate belongs to surgical diathermy; in therapeutic short-wave the risk is the implant sitting in the field between the applicator plates and concentrating current density.
fix: Say: the metal implant concentrates the electric field around it, raising local current density and causing a deep burn, and it may be inside the field between the plates. Keep the implant out of the treated volume or choose another method, following local safety rules.
